tagline: Tallgrass prairie and Osage Hills connect Pawhuska with the wider highway
intro: The Osage Nation Heritage Trail follows Highway 60 from Ponca City through Pawhuska to Bartlesville, crossing the Osage Hills. Oklahoma’s tourism department includes it among the state’s scenic byways and highlights tallgrass prairie and Osage Hills State Park’s rocky bluffs and forests. East of Ponca City, the highway crosses the Arkansas River, then runs 21 miles before its next state-highway junction southeast of Burbank. The Tallgrass Prairie Preserve lies north of Pawhuska. In town, the Osage Nation Museum brings together historical photographs and objects with both traditional and contemporary Osage art.

U.S. 60 reached Oklahoma through a westward extension approved in 1930. Here it replaced State Highway 11 between Ponca City and Pawhuska and State Highway 25 east toward Vinita. Later projects changed how travelers crossed the country: a 1952 rerouting bypassed Ponca City to the south and crossed a new Arkansas River bridge. In 1958, a straighter alignment replaced a curving section west of Pawhuska.

Travel east from Ponca City past the Burbank junction to Pawhuska, where the Osage Nation’s government remains based. From Pawhuska, U.S. 60 turns north, then east again toward the spur to Osage Hills State Park. Beyond the park turnoff, the road enters Bartlesville and follows Adams Boulevard through downtown.

moments.title: Burbank
moments.text: Burbank grew from a farming and ranching town of about 200 people into an oil-boom community of 3,000. E. W. Marland’s petroleum discovery northeast of town in May 1920 began that expansion. The Osage retained collective mineral rights and received royalties from the field, even as oil companies leased the land. Lease auctions usually took place beneath Pawhuska’s Million Dollar Elm, where oilmen including Marland, Frank Phillips and William G. Skelly bid. The field’s production peaked in 1923, then dropped by half in 1926. By 1930 the boom was over and the population had fallen to 372.

moments.title: Pawhuska
moments.text: The Osage Nation’s government opened offices in Pawhuska in 1872 and remains based here. The Osage Nation Museum, founded in 1938, holds photographs, historical objects, and traditional and contemporary art. Its collections include artifacts and documents donated by historian Louis F. Burns. The museum is the oldest tribally owned museum in the United States; the Nation also maintains archives and historic-preservation and cultural offices. Language work continues in the city, too: the Osage Nation governs Daposka Ahnkodapi Schools, which provides Osage-language immersion. The school opened in 2015, and incorporates the language into everyday routines.

moments.title: Osage Hills State Park
moments.text: A lone chimney, foundations and an amphitheater mark the former workers’ housing area at the north end of Osage Hills State Park. Civilian Conservation Corps construction began in 1935, making this one of Oklahoma’s seven original state parks. Workers used locally obtained stone and timber in their buildings. Eight guest cabins remain in use, with modernized interiors but their original appearance. A large picnic shelter has two stone fireplaces at opposite ends, another substantial piece of the park’s built landscape. Outside the buildings, hiking trails cross the park, and Sand Creek runs through its southern end.
